id: cpp-grid-dijkstra
title: Cheapest Path on a Terrain Grid
difficulty: Hard
order: 1
tags: priority_queue, Dijkstra, grids, path reconstruction
time_limit: 2
---
## Statement
A rover plans a path across an `R × C` terrain grid. Each cell holds an entry cost (a digit `1`–`9`) or `#` (impassable). Moving into a neighbouring cell (4 directions) costs that cell's digit. The start cell's own cost isn't paid.

Find the cheapest path from `S` (top-left, (0,0)) to `T` (bottom-right, (R-1, C-1)). Both are guaranteed to be digits. Print `cost X` and `steps K` (the number of moves on the path), then the grid with the path drawn using `*` (start and target included). If several cheapest paths exist, prefer the one with the fewest steps, and among those the one whose sequence of moves is lexicographically smallest in the order `D < L < R < U`. If T is unreachable, print `unreachable`.

R and C are up to 1000. Use Dijkstra with a `std::priority_queue`.

## Starter
```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <queue>
#include <string>

int main() {
    std::ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    std::cin.tie(nullptr);
    int R, C;
    std::cin >> R >> C;
    std::vector<std::string> g(R);
    for (auto& row : g) std::cin >> row;
}
```

## Hints
- Run Dijkstra **from T backwards**, using the cost of the cell you're moving *out of* towards T. Then `dist[cell]` is the cheapest cost from that cell to T. A second array holds the number of steps, as a tie-breaker in the priority `(cost, steps)`.
- Then walk forward from S: at each cell, among the neighbours `nb` in the order D, L, R, U, take the first with `dist[nb] + cost(nb) == dist[cur]` and `steps[nb] + 1 == steps[cur]`. This greedy walk produces the lexicographically smallest optimal move sequence.
- Push `(cost, steps, cell)` tuples into a min-heap (`std::greater<>`), and skip stale entries.

## Solution
```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <queue>
#include <string>
#include <tuple>
#include <climits>

int main() {
    std::ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    std::cin.tie(nullptr);
    int R, C;
    std::cin >> R >> C;
    std::vector<std::string> g(R);
    for (auto& row : g) std::cin >> row;

    const int N = R * C;
    auto cost = [&](int id) { return g[id / C][id % C] - '0'; };
    auto open = [&](int r, int c) { return r >= 0 && r < R && c >= 0 && c < C && g[r][c] != '#'; };
    const int dr[4] = {1, 0, 0, -1}, dc[4] = {0, -1, 1, 0};     // D L R U

    // backward Dijkstra from T: dist[v] = cheapest cost to go from v to T
    std::vector<long long> dist(N, LLONG_MAX);
    std::vector<int> steps(N, INT_MAX);
    using Item = std::tuple<long long, int, int>;                // cost, steps, cell
    std::priority_queue<Item, std::vector<Item>, std::greater<>> pq;
    int T = N - 1;
    dist[T] = 0;
    steps[T] = 0;
    pq.emplace(0, 0, T);
    while (!pq.empty()) {
        auto [d, s, u] = pq.top();
        pq.pop();
        if (d != dist[u] || s != steps[u]) continue;            // stale
        int ur = u / C, uc = u % C;
        for (int k = 0; k < 4; ++k) {
            int vr = ur + dr[k], vc = uc + dc[k];
            if (!open(vr, vc)) continue;
            int v = vr * C + vc;
            long long nd = d + cost(u);                         // moving v -> u pays cost(u)
            int ns = s + 1;
            if (nd < dist[v] || (nd == dist[v] && ns < steps[v])) {
                dist[v] = nd;
                steps[v] = ns;
                pq.emplace(nd, ns, v);
            }
        }
    }
    if (dist[0] == LLONG_MAX) { std::cout << "unreachable\n"; return 0; }

    std::cout << "cost " << dist[0] << "\nsteps " << steps[0] << '\n';
    int cur = 0;
    g[0][0] = '*';
    while (cur != T) {
        int r = cur / C, c = cur % C;
        for (int k = 0; k < 4; ++k) {
            int nr = r + dr[k], nc = c + dc[k];
            if (!open(nr, nc) && !(nr >= 0 && nr < R && nc >= 0 && nc < C && g[nr][nc] == '*')) continue;
            int nb = nr * C + nc;
            if (dist[nb] == LLONG_MAX || g[nr][nc] == '*') continue;
            if (dist[nb] + cost(nb) == dist[cur] && steps[nb] + 1 == steps[cur]) {
                cur = nb;
                break;
            }
        }
        g[cur / C][cur % C] = '*';
    }
    for (const auto& row : g) std::cout << row << '\n';
}
```

- **Dijkstra with a min-heap of tuples** `(cost, steps, cell)`: tuple comparison builds the secondary criterion (fewest steps) into the heap order for free, and `std::greater<>` turns the max-heap into a min-heap.
- **Lazy deletion:** improved distances are pushed again, and outdated heap entries are skipped when popped (there's no decrease-key in `priority_queue`).
- **Running the search backwards** gives every cell its exact cost-to-go. A greedy forward walk that always takes the first optimal neighbour in `D, L, R, U` order then yields the lexicographically smallest optimal path. This is the same "value function + greedy policy" structure as in robot motion planning (cost-to-go maps). The walk can't revisit a cell, because `steps` strictly decreases along it.
- Complexity: O(RC log(RC)), about 10⁶ · 20 operations.
